mechanism: ToFu reads each MCP tool's metadata, such as name, description and parameter schema, and picks matching checks from a CWE-guided corpus of sanitizers (path traversal, command injection and similar). It then generates a fuzzing harness per tool and uses runtime introspection to see what the tool actually did with the argument. Oracles judge the outcome, so a bug is confirmed by an observed effect, not a guess.
claim: Across 273 MCP servers and 3405 tools, verified bugs were found in 343 tools across 118 servers.
why_not_testable: The framework code is not confirmed released and a faithful slice needs running many third-party MCP servers.
needs: The ToFu code and a set of MCP servers to fuzz
one_line: Fuzzing 3405 MCP tools turned up verified bugs in 343 of them: tools trust whatever arguments the model hands over.
idea_why: Treating model-written arguments as untrusted input and fuzzing against documented schemas is standard security practice applied to a new boundary.
breakdown: List a server's tools through the MCP tools/list call, then for each parameter pick payloads from a sanitizer corpus matching its type. Call the tool in a sandbox, observe file, process and network effects, and flag violations of the documented input rules. Run it against servers the stack already uses to check what Proteus trusts. A security reviewer would triage which findings are real.

mechanism: Each problem fixes an integer function with known values only at small n and keeps a lower and an upper record, each a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof. A submission must prove it bounds f, is no worse than the record anywhere and is strictly better somewhere, then becomes the new record. Two independent Lean kernels check every proof, and checks reject functions that just brute-force small n.
claim: Agents had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record, then 60 more from newer models improved 19 of 20 records again.
why_not_testable: Needs a Lean toolchain and the released problem set, and a meaningful submission takes agent hours.
needs: Lean 4 toolchain and the benchmark release
one_line: A benchmark that ratchets: every accepted Lean proof becomes the new record to beat, so it never saturates.
idea_why: Making the verifier the judge and the record the moving bar removes both saturation and referee trust.
breakdown: Install Lean 4 and mathlib, load a problem's current records and the admission tool, then have an agent propose a better bound function with a proof. Run the checker and two kernels, and on acceptance replace the record. The same ratchet pattern could score a Proteus desk: a pre-registered rule must beat the current best on a fixed test to replace it.
